In a galaxy cluster, the 30–100 million °C gas between the galaxies holds more mass than all of the cluster’s galaxies put together.
Black holes are not cosmic vacuum cleaners: from far enough away, a black hole’s gravity acts just like that of any other object with the same mass.
By the time the first gravitational waves LIGO caught reached Earth, the wobble they caused in spacetime was 10,000 times smaller than an atomic nucleus.
The 1995 Hubble Deep Field stared for 10 days at a patch of sky about 1/13 the width of the full Moon and revealed roughly 3,000 galaxies.
Charles Messier once mistook the Crab Nebula for Halley’s Comet, and the mix-up inspired his famous list of fuzzy objects that comet hunters could ignore.
Because Earth bulges at the equator, the summit of Ecuador's Chimborazo is the point farthest from Earth's centre, about 2 km farther out than the top of Everest.
Earth is the densest planet in the solar system, averaging about 5.5 grams per cubic centimetre, roughly five and a half times the density of water.
The thermosphere can heat up to around 2,000 degrees Celsius when the Sun is very active, yet its air is so thin that the International Space Station orbits inside it.
Earth's north magnetic pole is on the move: it has wandered from the Canadian Arctic toward Siberia, recently at around 50 km a year.
Earth's outermost atmosphere, a faint glow of hydrogen called the geocorona, stretches out to about 630,000 km, almost twice the distance to the Moon.
From its post a million miles away, the DSCOVR spacecraft has photographed the Moon crossing in front of Earth, showing the fully lit lunar far side that can never be seen from the ground.
All seven planets of TRAPPIST-1 orbit closer to their star than Mercury does to the Sun, and their years last between about 1.5 and 19 days.
For its main mission, Kepler stared at about 150,000 stars in one patch of sky in the constellation Cygnus, and it left a legacy of more than 2,600 planet discoveries.
Statistics from Kepler suggest the Milky Way has more planets than stars, which would mean more than a trillion planets in our galaxy alone.
The hot Jupiter WASP-12 b is being eaten by its star: it is stretched into a football shape, its swollen atmosphere spills onto the star, and it may have only about 10 million years left.
Webb's first direct image of an exoplanet, taken in 2022, showed HIP 65426 b, a young gas giant more than 10,000 times fainter than its star in near-infrared light.
TESS flies an unusual orbit lasting 13.7 days, locked in a 2:1 rhythm with the Moon, which keeps the orbit stable for many years.
In 1998, aged 77, John Glenn returned to orbit aboard Space Shuttle Discovery, 36 years after his first flight, and doctors studied how spaceflight affected an older body.
At the end of Apollo 15, David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather on the Moon on live TV, and with no air to slow the feather, both hit the ground together.
The space station's life support recycles about 98 percent of the water crews use, including moisture from their breath and sweat and even urine.
Across six landings, Apollo astronauts brought back about 382 kilograms of Moon rocks, core samples and soil, still studied by scientists today.
People have lived aboard the International Space Station without a break since November 2000, so nobody born after that date has known a time with no humans in orbit.
Valentina Tereshkova's single flight in 1963 lasted almost three days, more time in space than all American Mercury astronauts who had flown up to then combined.
After the first spacewalk, Alexei Leonov's suit had ballooned so much that he could not fit back into the airlock until he let some of the air out of it.
The Soviet commander of the 1975 Apollo-Soyuz docking, the first joint US-Soviet crewed flight, was Alexei Leonov, who had made the first spacewalk ten years earlier.
By late 2026 Voyager 1 is about one light-day from Earth: a command sent at the speed of light needs roughly a full day to reach it.
A tiny swatch of muslin from the Wright brothers' 1903 Flyer was tucked under the solar panel of the Ingenuity helicopter, so a piece of the first aeroplane also flew on Mars.
Hubble circles Earth about once every 95 minutes and has completed more than 195,000 orbits since 1990.
Each of the five layers of Webb's tennis-court-sized sunshield is thinner than a sheet of paper, yet together they keep the telescope side about 300 degrees Celsius colder than the Sun-facing side.
The icy jets Cassini found on Saturn's small moon Enceladus feed one of the planet's rings: the wide, faint E ring is made mostly of ice from that moon.
At its closest to the Sun, Parker Solar Probe moves at about 700,000 km/h, fast enough to cross from London to New York in under 30 seconds.
New Horizons carries some of the ashes of Clyde Tombaugh, the astronomer who discovered Pluto in 1930, so he finally passed by the world he found.
NEAR Shoemaker was never designed to land, yet in 2001 it touched down gently on asteroid Eros and kept sending data from the surface.
About 500 years ago, Leonardo da Vinci worked out that the faint glow on the dark part of a crescent Moon is sunlight reflected back from Earth.
If Betelgeuse, the red star at Orion’s shoulder, took the Sun’s place, its surface would reach far beyond the orbit of Mars.
Polaris will not always be the North Star: Earth's axis slowly wobbles, and in about 12,000 years it will point near the bright star Vega instead.
Total solar eclipses are a cosmic coincidence: the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon but also about 400 times farther away, so both look almost the same size.
Most shooting stars are made by bits of comet dust no bigger than a grain of sand or a pea, burning up high in the atmosphere.
Perseid meteors hit the upper atmosphere at about 59 km per second, fast enough to cover the length of Great Britain in under 20 seconds.
After the Sun and the Moon, the International Space Station can be the brightest object in the sky, and it needs no telescope to spot.
The planets always appear along the same narrow band of sky, the ecliptic, because they all orbit the Sun in nearly the same flat plane.
